name: Claim Check
intent: Store a large payload somewhere else and send only a small ticket through the message channel.
scenario: Users upload videos of up to 20 MB, and each upload is announced to a processing service through a message queue whose messages are limited to 256 KB.
problem: The producer puts the whole video into the queue message. The message is larger than the queue allows, so it is rejected, and even where it is allowed the queue is slow and expensive because every hop copies the video.
solution: The producer stores the video in blob storage and gets back an id, the claim check. It sends a tiny message that contains only that id. The consumer reads the message, uses the id to fetch the video from storage, processes it, and deletes it when it is done. The queue carries tickets, and the storage carries the heavy data.
pain: The message is larger than the queue accepts and is rejected
Every hop and every consumer copies the whole video
The queue's memory and bandwidth are used up by a few big messages
Slow big messages delay the small ones behind them
benefits: Messages stay tiny, whatever the size of the data
The queue stays fast and its cost stays low
Only the consumer that needs the payload downloads it
Storage is built for large objects and scales on its own
whenToUse: The payload is large, or may be large, compared with the queue's limits
Many consumers read the message but only one needs the payload
Messages pass through several hops that would each copy the data
whenNotToUse: Small messages: a storage round trip costs more than sending the data inline
When the data must travel and be deleted atomically with the message
When you cannot add and operate a storage service just for this
pitfalls: Orphaned blobs: if a consumer crashes before deleting the payload, nothing removes it, so storage grows
The message and the blob can go out of step: the message arrives before the blob is readable, or the blob expires first
The ticket is a reference, not a copy: whoever holds it can read the data, so access must be controlled
Two network calls (a put and a get) are added to every message

roles.label: Producer
roles.description: Stores the large payload and sends a message that holds only its id.

roles.label: Payload store
roles.description: Blob storage that holds the payload until it is claimed and deleted.

roles.label: Claim-check message
roles.description: A small message that carries the ticket (the id), not the data.

roles.label: Consumer
roles.description: Reads the message, fetches the payload with the ticket, processes it and deletes it.

quiz.question: A queue accepts messages of up to 256 KB, but uploaded videos are up to 20 MB. Processing must be started through the queue. What is the best design?
options: Split each video into 80 pieces that fit, and send the pieces as separate messages
Store the video in blob storage and send a message that holds only its id
Compress each video so that it fits under 256 KB before it is sent to the queue
Ask the queue provider to raise the limit to 25 MB, so that videos fit in a message
quiz.explanation: A claim check keeps messages tiny while storage holds the video. Splitting needs reassembly, and the pieces still go through the queue. Compression cannot guarantee 256 KB, and a higher limit still copies the video through every hop.

quiz.question: A claim-check system keeps growing its storage bill. Consumers sometimes crash after fetching a video and before deleting it, and nothing else removes the blob. What is the best fix?
options: Never delete videos, and move old ones to cheaper storage after a month
Make consumers delete the blob before they fetch it, so that it can never be left behind
Delete the blob only after successful processing, and add an expiry rule for blobs that nothing claims
Keep each video inside the queue message as well, so that a copy always exists for retries
quiz.explanation: Delete after success so that a retry can still fetch the data, and let a retention rule remove what is never claimed. Keeping everything or deleting before fetching loses either money or data, and putting the video in the message brings back the original problem.

quiz.question: A team applies the claim check to every message in the system for consistency, including 2 KB status updates. What is the likely result?
options: Every small message pays for a storage write and read it did not need, so small ones should stay inline
The system gets faster, because every message is now the same small size
The queue becomes safer, because no message ever holds user data inside it
The storage service is used less, because tickets are shared between many messages
quiz.explanation: The pattern exists to avoid moving large payloads. For a 2 KB message it only adds two network calls and a blob to clean up. Use it when the payload is large or may be, and send the rest inline.
